# Review a pull request

`<skill folder>` below means the folder that holds this SKILL.md; use its full path. This skill uses the daily-review skill installed next to it, in `<skill folder>/../daily-review`.

## What changes for a pull request
Review the pull request exactly as $daily-review reviews a day's commits: the purpose, what to look for, the report and the follow-ups are daily-review's, included at the end. Two things change: the PR's code is checked out in a worktree of its own, and the findings also go on the PR as a pending review, which only the lead sees until they submit it on GitHub.

**Fetch the PR.** Run `bash <skill folder>/scripts/pr.sh "<PR link or number>"`, adding any `--rerun`, `--full`, `--clean`, `--since REF` or `--days N` from the user's message. It calls GitHub and writes to `.git` (the PR's commits and its worktree), so run it outside Codex's sandbox, with the lead's approval. It checks the PR out in a worktree inside the lead's checkout without touching their branch, then prints the PR's details and daily-review's scope for it. With `--clean`, pr.sh only removes PR worktrees (the logs stay): tell the lead what it removed and stop. If it reports `status: error`, tell the lead in a line and stop. If the scope says `nothing-new`, tell the lead, and if `previous_draft` was never posted, offer to post it.

**Review it as daily-review does**, with these differences:
- The scope comes from pr.sh, which also takes the flags.
- The PR's code is in `worktree`. Read, search and list files there: the lead's own checkout is on another branch, and a search of the whole checkout skips the worktree. For git, name the commits from the scope rather than relying on HEAD: `git show <head>:<path>`, `git blame <head> -- <path>`, `git grep <pattern> <head>`. Never run the PR's code, tests or build scripts: a pull request can carry code that shouldn't run on the lead's machine, above all one from a fork. Brief any subagent the same way.
- `description` holds the PR's title and description: the developer's account of what the PR does and why. Use it as the stated intent and check it against the code. `checks` gives the CI results for the PR's head: evidence about the code (for example, whether the tests pass), not findings to repeat, since the developer sees them on GitHub.
- `existing_comments` holds what others have already said on the PR. The report covers every finding, but on GitHub don't repeat a point someone has made: when it is still unresolved at the PR's head, add only what they missed, and say whose point you are building on (by name, without an @, so they aren't notified again).
- REVIEW.md is the file named in the scope's `review_md`, chosen so that a PR can't change the rules it is reviewed against. If the PR edits REVIEW.md, report the edit as a [lead] decision. If there is no REVIEW.md, or its sources aren't confirmed, settle them with the lead as daily-review says and keep REVIEW.md in the lead's own checkout (the folder that holds `.reviews/`), never in the worktree.
- `branch_review`, when pr.sh prints it, is the lead's last $daily-review of the PR's branch, from before this PR's first review. Treat it as the previous review for numbering and open items, while still reviewing the whole PR.
- `--architecture` belongs to $daily-review only.

**Write the GitHub draft** to `github_draft` after saving the report. It is what the developer will read on the PR:

```
# Summary
<the review's opening comment>

# Comments
## <path>:<line>
<an inline comment>

## <path>:<first line>-<last line>
<a comment on several lines>
```

- A finding or a [developer] decision about particular lines of the PR's diff becomes an inline comment on those lines. `commentable_lines` lists the lines GitHub accepts comments on; lines marked + are the ones the PR adds or changes. Start the comment with `**#<n> · Must fix · <headline>**` (or Should fix, Minor, Decision), then the explanation and the fix as in the report, without the location, which GitHub shows.
- When the fix is a small, exact replacement, add it as a `suggestion` code block, which the developer can apply with one click. It replaces exactly the commented lines, so the heading's line range must match the lines it replaces, indentation included.
- Everything else goes in the summary, labelled the same way and with the report's numbers where it has them: missing tests, problems that span files or sit outside the diff, and [developer] decisions not tied to a line. Open the summary with what has to change before the PR can merge, in a line or two, without repeating the inline comments. Items still open from an earlier review of this PR were posted then: list their numbers in one line, with a few words where only part was fixed, and the numbers fixed since. Items carried over from `branch_review` have never been on GitHub, so post them like new findings. When there is nothing to report, one line saying so is enough; approving is the lead's call.
- Leave out what is only for the lead: [lead] and [client] decisions, notes about the plan, Spec changed. If the PR has to wait for one of those decisions, say that it waits on a decision about it.
- Write to the developer in plain words, without praise or em-dashes.

**Post it.** Check the draft with `python3 <skill folder>/scripts/post_review.py --dry-run <github_draft>`. It lists comments it had to shrink to the diff or move to the summary: correct any line you got wrong, and leave a comment in the summary when its problem really is outside the diff. When the user's message includes `--dry-run`, stop there and tell the lead where the draft is. Otherwise post with `python3 <skill folder>/scripts/post_review.py <github_draft>`, outside the sandbox because it calls GitHub: the lead's approval of that command is their go-ahead to post. It creates a pending review and never submits, approves or requests changes.

Then tell the lead, in a few lines, where the report is saved with daily-review's counts per part, what went to GitHub, and what you need from them. For example: "Saved the review to `.reviews/pr-42/review-1-2026-10-29_1830.md`. Backend: 2 must fix, 1 minor; 2 decisions for you. Posted a pending review with 3 inline comments and 2 items in the summary: <link>. Only you can see it until you submit it from the PR's Files changed tab." Mention anything the script moved, shrank or warned about. If the script says they already have a pending review on this PR, tell them, and use `--replace-pending` only when they ask for it: it deletes that pending review, including any comments they added to it on GitHub.

## After posting
- To change a posted review, edit the draft and post again with `--replace-pending`, once the lead confirms their pending review holds nothing they want to keep. They can also edit or delete the comments on GitHub before submitting.
- When the lead is done with the PR, `bash <skill folder>/scripts/pr.sh --clean <number>`, run outside the sandbox, removes its worktree (without a number, every PR's). The review logs stay in `.reviews/pr-<number>/`.
- daily-review's follow-ups below apply as well.

# From $daily-review

## What this is for
The user is the tech lead. The developers may use other tools, so they never see this session: the lead reads your review at the end of the day and forwards it to them. The lead wants two things from this skill: feedback that gets to the point instead of a long document, and the issues that matter for this project. Everything else is how you would normally work in a repository: understand the change before you judge it, read the code around it, and ask the lead when you need something only they know.

## Getting oriented
The scope lists the commits since the last review, the changed files, the diff file, the sources of truth and the previous review. If the status is `nothing-new` or `error`, tell the lead in a line and stop.

Read `REVIEW.md` first. It says who does what on this project, which documents are the sources of truth, what stage the project is at and what matters most here. The decisions file, when there is one, lists what the lead has asked the review not to flag. Sources are files in this repository, so everyone works from the same version. Word files are converted to text for you (follow the `-> read` path), and a source listed under `specs_newer_on_base` should be read from the base branch. If there is no REVIEW.md, if it says `Sources confirmed: no`, or if the scope lists missing sources or `doc_candidates`, agree with the lead which documents to review against before anything else, and record it in REVIEW.md (start a new one from `<skill folder>/../daily-review/templates/REVIEW.template.md`). Never keep a copy of a source outside the repository.

Then understand what was done: read the commit messages and the diff, the code around each change and what it calls, and the parts of the sources that cover this work. Work out which part of the plan or which task it implements, and whether it is developer work at all. A commit that only changes the plan or the architecture docs is the lead's own design work: ask what they want from the review rather than reviewing it like code.

Before you write the report, ask the lead (in one go) about anything you can't settle from the code and the docs that would change what you report: what the work is meant to do, whether a departure from the plan was agreed, whether something is in scope yet. Don't ask what REVIEW.md, the docs or the code already answer. A line or two telling the lead what you're reviewing and how is welcome.

## What to look for
What a strong senior engineer on this project would block or comment on in a pull request:
- Work that doesn't do what the plan or the task says for this feature, or contradicts it.
- Bugs and missed edge cases on reachable paths: empty, missing or unexpected input, errors swallowed or reported as success, half-finished writes, races and retries, dates and time zones.
- Security and privacy: role checks only in the UI, one customer's or tenant's data reachable by another, personal or secret data in logs, errors, URLs, analytics or browser storage.
- Changed behavior without tests, above all for auth, permissions, tenancy and data writes.
- Design that won't hold at the scale in REVIEW.md, with a rough estimate of why.
- Questions the plan doesn't answer that this work had to decide: recommend an answer and say who should decide (the developer, the lead or the client).
- Edits to the sources made in these commits: what changed, and anything it now conflicts with.

Leave out formatting, lint and type errors (hooks catch them), matters of taste, features the plan puts in a later phase, problems in code these commits didn't touch unless the new code depends on them, and anything REVIEW.md or the decisions file excludes.

For a large change you can hand parts of the reading to `daily-reviewer` subagents (by area, or by plan, correctness and design), passing on your understanding of the change and anything the lead told you. What they return are candidates; you decide what is real. Before you report, try to prove each finding wrong against the code, and when you have more than a couple of findings or any you're unsure about, have a `review-verifier` subagent check them with fresh eyes. A wrong finding costs the lead and the developer a round trip. In Codex, spawn them as subagents and give each its instructions, `<skill folder>/../daily-review/references/daily-reviewer.md` or `<skill folder>/../daily-review/references/review-verifier.md`, with your brief. Subagents share your sandbox, so tell them not to edit files. If you can't spawn subagents, do their checks yourself, following the same instructions.

## The report
Start with this line:

```
**Review** `<branch>` <base7>..<head7> · <n> commits · <m> files
```

When REVIEW.md splits the codebase into parts (for example backend and frontend), give each part its own heading (`## Backend`, `## Frontend`) with only its findings under it, so each developer gets a separate list. An item that needs changes in more than one part goes under the part where the problem starts and says what the other part must change. Leave out a part these commits didn't touch; for a part they touched with nothing to report, write `All good.` under its heading. Without parts, the sections follow the first line directly.

Within each part, these sections in this order, leaving out empty ones:
- **Must fix**: breaks behavior on a reachable path, a security or privacy hole, data loss, or contradicts the plan for this feature.
- **Should fix**: a real problem that is less likely or less costly.
- **Missing tests**: one line per file, naming what isn't tested and the cases.
- **Minor**: harmless today but worth fixing; five at most.
- **Still open** from earlier reviews: one line each, with the number, the date first flagged, the location and a short title.

After the parts, the sections about the change as a whole:
- **Decisions needed**: what the plan doesn't settle, each starting with who decides: [developer], [lead] or [client]. Problems in the plan or the architecture docs themselves go here too, as [lead] items.
- **Spec changed** in this range: one line per source.

Numbers run across the whole report, so each number means one item. Then, when they apply: `Open decisions: #n (date, owner)`, `Tests still missing: <path> (<count>)` and `Fixed since <date>: #n, #n`. When there is nothing to report at all, the whole report is one line: ``All good. `<branch>` <base7>..<head7>, <n> commits.``

Write each finding so a junior developer can act on it without opening the plan: a bold headline saying what goes wrong and for whom, then why in plain words, naming the variables, functions or columns involved where that helps, then the fix, then the location and plan section. Keep it as short as that allows, with no praise and no description of code that is fine. For example:

```
16. **A discount code larger than the order makes the total negative, and checkout refunds the customer.** `apply_discount` subtracts `code.amount` from `order.total` with no floor, so a $20 code on a $15 order saves `total = -5`, and the payment step treats it as a $5 refund. This commit added fixed-amount codes but kept the arithmetic written for percentage codes.
    Fix: use `max(order.total - code.amount, 0)` and reject the code when it exceeds the order. (`api/orders/discounts.py:58`, plan 4.2)

17. [lead] **Nothing says what happens to a team's projects when the owner deletes their account.** This commit adds account deletion, and `delete_user` leaves the owner's projects with `owner_id = NULL`, which the dashboard query skips, so the rest of the team loses access to them. The plan covers deleting an account but not handing projects over.
    Recommend: block deleting an owner who still has projects until ownership is transferred, and add a transfer endpoint. Update plan 6.3 once decided.
```

Numbers identify items across days: continue from the highest number in the previous review, and carried-over items keep theirs. If there is a previous review, check each of its open items against the current code (yourself or through the `review-verifier`): fixed, still open, or gone with the code. Decisions stay open until the docs cover them or the lead drops them; Minor and Spec changed items don't carry over.

Save the report to `log_file`: the `log_frontmatter` lines exactly as printed, a blank line, then the report. Don't repeat the report in the conversation: tell the lead where you saved it, with one line of counts per part (for example "Backend: 2 must fix, 5 should fix. Frontend: 1 should fix. 1 decision"), plus anything you need from them. An All good review is still saved.

## After the report
- When the lead says a finding is intended or wrong ("#3 is fine", "don't flag X"), add one line to `.reviews/decisions.md`: `- <date> <path or area>: <what not to flag> (<reason>)`. If it applies to the whole team, suggest adding it to REVIEW.md under Known decisions.
- "Message for the developer": rewrite the findings as a message to the developer in plain words, without em-dashes; one message per part when the report has parts.
- Don't change the project's code unless the lead asks.

## Files
`.reviews/` is kept out of git (`.git/info/exclude`): one file per review in `.reviews/<branch>/`, named `review-<n>-<date>_<HHMM>.md`, architecture reviews in `.reviews/architecture/`, `decisions.md`, and scratch files in `.work/`. `scripts/scope.sh` picks the commit range, writes the diff and converts Word sources to text with `scripts/docx2md.py`.
